summary:
The Jakarta Special Capital Region stands under the national framework of Indonesia, which is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, this provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national-level morality provisions. In Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025; those punishments reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors.

Venue raids are a standing enforcement instrument. On 22 June 2025, Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena described the operation as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering violated no law.

There is a directly documented death of a trans traveler in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022. During a WhatsApp call, his mother in Lima was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; his mother alleges that police beat him, while Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.

Official policy frames LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists nonmilitary threats and places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled. Reporting from August 2026 ties that framing to a wave of vigilante attacks on transgender women, with mobs attacking trans people as the government codifies anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes into law. Commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.

Jakarta is the most heavily raided venue in Indonesia for LGBTQ+ gatherings, and the capital's raid series is the clearest documented instance of the national pattern. Police arrested 141 people over a "gay sex party" in Jakarta in May 2017, detained 144 at the Atlantis Gym sauna on 21 May 2017 with ten subsequently charged, and arrested 51 at a Central Jakarta sauna in October 2017 with six charged. All of those cases were pursued under the pornography law.

The same pattern continues in the current period. Police detained 56 people at a hotel in South Jakarta on 1 February 2025, nine at another South Jakarta hotel on 24 May 2025, and 75 at a private villa near the capital on 22 June 2025. Offences charged in these operations can carry up to 15 years' imprisonment under Indonesia's broadly worded Pornography Law.

Arrests in these raids are made without naming detainees and without judicial proceedings, according to Amnesty International's 24 June 2025 press release. Amnesty International Indonesia's deputy director called the villa operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy that exemplifies the hostile environment for LGBTI people in Indonesia, and demanded the release of those arrested.

There is no LGBT-specific statute and no general anti-discrimination law in Indonesia, so police action in Jakarta operates on pornography and morality provisions rather than any LGBT-specific offence. A visitor therefore faces exposure through broadly worded national laws applied at the discretion of police, not through a named prohibition.
tangentialFactors:
Jakarta is one of eight provinces where an international NGO found discriminatory regional regulations, and at the same time the city with the country's densest LGBTQ+ infrastructure, media presence and monitoring-group offices. An assessor should expect both to be true at once: organised visibility and organised repression coexist in the same city.

An October 2025 presidential decree named "the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture" a non-military national security threat alongside terrorism, radicalism and drug addiction. Journalists report a constant chilling effect, with editors killing LGBTQ+ stories for fear of state reprisal or religious backlash, and civil-society and independent media space has contracted since 2024-25. That contraction is documented amid student-led anti-government protests, so the hostility is not confined to sexual politics.

The August 2026 reporting on vigilante attacks against transgender women indicates that the security-decree framing has consequences on the street as well as in policy, raising the risk of mob violence against visibly trans people independent of any police encounter.

Compared with Aceh, where religious law produces public caning, Jakarta's exposure is administrative and criminal rather than corporal: detention, prosecution under the pornography law, and in 2018 the use of city-run detention facilities. The practical difference for a visitor is the form of the penalty, not its likelihood.
localsOnly:
In March 2018 the Jakarta Social Agency declared transgender waria "socially dysfunctional" and detained trans women in city-run "rehabilitation" centres unless they signed statements promising not to repeat their "offence". This is a municipal administrative measure available to Jakarta authorities outside the criminal process.

Transgender people in Indonesia may change legal gender only after surgery and a judge's approval. There is no general anti-discrimination law, so there is no statutory basis on which a trans resident can claim protection in employment, housing or public services.

Residents who attend private gatherings face the same pornography-law exposure as visitors: the 2017 and 2025 Jakarta detentions were of people present at private or semi-private events, and the charges available to prosecutors reach up to 15 years' imprisonment.
